tip: 'Niemand' adds '-en' in the accusative: 'er kennt niemanden in dieser Stadt'.
Separable verb: 'aufgeben' becomes 'aufgegeben' with 'ge-' slotted between the prefix and the stem.
The verb 'gefallen' takes a dative object: 'dem Kind'. German frames it as the gift being pleasing to the child.
'Verzeihen' takes dative for the person and accusative for the thing: 'seinem Freund den peinlichen Fehler'.
'Schmeicheln' (to flatter) takes a dative object: 'das Kompliment schmeichelt der jungen Künstlerin'.
Some adjectives pair with a dative person: 'ist mir wichtig' means is important to me.
A modal verb pushes the main verb to the clause end as an infinitive: 'kann' up front, 'tragen' at the end.
After 'in', motion toward a place takes the accusative: 'in seine Heimatstadt', not 'seiner'.
'Nach Hause' means homeward, 'zu Hause' means at home: 'mit nach Hause nehmen' is take home with you.
'Trotz' takes the genitive case: 'trotz des Regens' means despite the rain.
With a separable verb, 'zu' slots inside it: 'anrufen' becomes 'anzurufen'.
'Ein paar' means a few and never changes its ending: 'ein paar Münzen'.
A time span takes the accusative with no preposition: 'das gesamte Wochenende'.
'Sich nähern' (to approach) takes a dative object: 'wir nähern uns dem Gipfel'.
'Ähneln' (to resemble) takes dative with no preposition: 'er ähnelt seiner Mutter'.
'Darf ... nicht' means must not, a prohibition: entering the building is forbidden. 'Muss nicht' instead means need not.
'Ob' means whether and pushes its verb to the end: 'ob das Restaurant heute geöffnet hat' lands 'hat' at the close of the clause.
'Zwischen' takes dative for a fixed location: 'zwischen der Post und dem Rathaus' marks where something sits. Motion toward would switch it to accusative.
'Nicht' vs 'kein': use 'keinen Kaffee' (negating noun) but 'nicht einschlafen' (negating verb).
'Servus' is common in Bavaria and Austria – both greeting and farewell.
'Hinter' takes dative for a standing-still position: 'steht hinter dem Zaun'. Moving to behind the fence would flip it to accusative, 'den Zaun'.
'Grüß Gott' is a standard greeting in southern Germany and Austria.
'Gegenüber' means across from and takes the dative: 'gegenüber dem Park'.
'Länger' is the comparative of 'lang': add '-er' plus an umlaut, as many short adjectives do.
Time phrases like 'heute Abend' take no preposition; say it directly, not 'am heute Abend'.
The prefix 'zer-' is inseparable and adds a sense of breaking apart, so 'zerstörte' keeps the prefix attached.
Instruments normally drop the article with 'spielen': 'Klavier spielen' means play the piano, not 'das Klavier spielen'.
The ending '-erweise' turns an adjective into a comment on the whole sentence: 'Unglücklicherweise' means unfortunately.
'Sich nähern' takes a dative object: 'dem scheuen Reh'.
'Antworten' takes dative for the person: 'dem Professor'.
